mainTopic: Rolling back a fallen ספר on שבת: who authored the משנה, אביי's כרמלית explanation of the four-אמות rule, and the reader on the roof who turns the scroll over.
overview: The משנה lets a person reading on a threshold roll a ספר back to himself on שבת, even though this seems to involve a rabbinic prohibition (שבות). The גמרא first says the משנה follows רבי שמעון, who holds that a שבות gives way for כתבי הקודש. רב יהודה accepts that this splits the משנה between רבי שמעון and רבי יהודה. רבה instead explains the leniency as a special allowance to prevent בזיון on a threshold people walk on. אביי rejects this from a ברייתא that draws a line at four אמות. He explains that the threshold is a כרמלית in front of a רשות הרבים, so within four אמות only a rabbinic violation is at stake. The גמרא then worries that he might carry the ספר straight into the house. It answers with a long threshold, a pause to look at the scrolls, בן עזאי's rule that walking counts as standing, and the rule that one does not throw holy writings. Next, the גמרא explains why the reader on a roof may turn the scroll face-down: it is the lesser disgrace. רבא sets that case on a slanted wall, and when אביי challenges him from רבי יהודה's ruling, the גמרא says the משנה is missing words. The fuller reading continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The משנה follows רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers its earlier question. The משנה follows רבי שמעון, who holds that a rabbinic prohibition does not stand in the way of protecting כתבי הקודש.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who is the author of this משנה? It is רבי שמעון, who said: anything forbidden only because of a rabbinic שבות does not stand in the way of saving holy writings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks who wrote this משנה. It answers that it is רבי שמעון, and that explains why rolling the ספר back is allowed even though it involves a rabbinic prohibition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem was that rolling the ספר back seemed to break a rabbinic rule (שבות). The answer is that for רבי שמעון, a rabbinic rule gives way when holy writings are at stake. So the משנה's leniency is no longer a problem, as long as רבי שמעון is the author.

keyTerms.meaning: Who is it? (Who is the author of this teaching?)
A rabbinic prohibition on שבת meant to protect the day's restful character
Does not stand in the way of (gives way to)
Holy writings (ספרי תנ״ך)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole סוגיא. The rest of the discussion tests whether רבי שמעון can really be the author of the entire משנה.

phrases.english: Who is it (the author)?
It is Rabbi Shimon, who said:
Anything that is forbidden only because of a rabbinic decree
does not stand in the way of holy writings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem raised on the previous amud: moving the ספר seems to involve a שבות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Attributing the משנה to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seems to permit something that is rabbinically forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: It follows רבי שמעון, for whom a שבות gives way for כתבי הקודש.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי שמעון, a rabbinic שבות does not override the protection of holy writings.

steps.title: The end of the משנה shows the middle clause cannot be רבי שמעון
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the end of the משנה, where רבי שמעון is very lenient. The stricter middle clause therefore cannot be his, so the משנה would switch authors in the middle.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the end of the משנה: רבי יהודה says that even if the ספר is only a thread's width off the ground, he rolls it back to himself. רבי שמעון says that even if it is on the ground itself, he rolls it back. So the first and last clauses are רבי שמעון, but the middle clause is רבי יהודה?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer in step 1. It quotes the end of the משנה to show that the middle clause does not fit רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the end of the משנה, רבי שמעון allows rolling the ספר back even when it is lying on the ground. The middle clause (about reading on a roof) is stricter: once the ספר comes within ten טפחים of the ground, you may not roll it back and must turn it over instead. That strict clause cannot be רבי שמעון's. So if the beginning is רבי שמעון, the משנה would jump from one author to another and back, which is an awkward reading.

keyTerms.meaning: Look at (say) the last clause
The width of a thread
He rolls it back to himself
The first clause
The middle clause

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether רבי שמעון is lenient. The problem is that the middle clause is strict, so one משנה would have to be split between two authors.

phrases.english: Say (look at) the last clause:
Rabbi Yehuda says:
Even if it is not removed from the ground
more than a thread's width, he rolls it back to himself.
Rabbi Shimon says:
Even if it is on the ground itself, he rolls it back to himself.
So the first and last clauses are Rabbi Shimon,
and the middle clause is Rabbi Yehuda?!
phrases.notes: Said as an exclamation of difficulty.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges step 1's claim that רבי שמעון is the author.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the משנה follows רבי שמעון
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The middle clause is stricter than רבי שמעון's stated view, so the משנה would have to be split among authors.

steps.title: רב יהודה accepts the split authorship
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה simply agrees that the משנה is split: the first and last clauses follow רבי שמעון, and the middle clause follows רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: Yes. The first and last clauses are רבי שמעון, and the middle clause is רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה answers the challenge by accepting it. The משנה really does switch authors in the middle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of looking for a way around the problem, רב יהודה says the unusual reading is correct. This keeps the answer from step 1: the first clause is רבי שמעון, so a שבות gives way for holy writings.

keyTerms.meaning: Yes (Aramaic)

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said: Yes,
the first and last clauses are Rabbi Shimon,
the middle clause is Rabbi Yehuda.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 2 by accepting its conclusion.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Biting the bullet (accepting the split authorship)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A משנה should not switch authors in the middle.
steps.terutzMaskana: This משנה does switch: first and last clauses רבי שמעון, middle clause רבי יהודה.

steps.title: רבה: a threshold people walk on, permitted to prevent disgrace
steps.stepSummary: רבה gives a different explanation. The case is a threshold that people walk over, and the חכמים permitted rolling the ספר back so the holy writings would not be disgraced.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: Here we are dealing with a threshold that people walk on. Because of the disgrace to the holy writings, the חכמים permitted it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה offers another way to explain the משנה, so that it does not need to depend on רבי שמעון.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה agrees that rolling the ספר back involves a rabbinic prohibition. But on a threshold that people walk on, the ספר would be trampled, and that is a special reason for a leniency. Because of this concern, even the other חכמים, not only רבי שמעון, would allow it, so the משנה does not need to be split.

keyTerms.meaning: A threshold that people step on
Disgrace, disrespect
The חכמים permitted it
We are dealing with

steps.confusionAlert: רבה does not say there is no prohibition at all. He says the חכמים made an exception to their own rule because of the disgrace.

phrases.english: Rabba said:
Here we are dealing with a threshold that is stepped on,
and because of disgrace to the holy writings
the Sages permitted it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּה אָמַר: הָכָא בְּאִיסְקוּפָּה הַנִּדְרֶסֶת עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different answer from steps 1 and 3 to the original problem of the שבות.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The leniency must come from רבי שמעון's general rule.
steps.terutzMaskana: The leniency comes from a special exception the חכמים made against בזיון on a threshold people walk on.

steps.title: אביי challenges רבה from the four-amos distinction
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a ברייתא that allows rolling the ספר back only within four אמות; beyond that, one turns it face down. If the reason were disgrace on a walked-on threshold, distance should make no difference.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי challenged him: Within four אמות, he rolls it back to himself; beyond four, he turns it over onto its writing. If you say we are dealing with a threshold people walk on, what difference does it make whether it is within four אמות or beyond four אמות?
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's explanation from step 4, using a ברייתא that draws a line at four אמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the only reason for the leniency is to keep the ספר from being trampled, that danger exists at any distance. Yet the ברייתא permits rolling it back only within four אמות, and beyond that requires turning it face down. This suggests the leniency is based on something other than disgrace, which weakens רבה's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection against him (from a ברייתא)
Four אמות, a halachic measure of distance
He turns it over onto its writing (face down)
What difference does it make to me?

phrases.english: Abaye raised an objection to him:
Within four cubits, he rolls it back to himself;
beyond four, he turns it over onto its writing.
And if you say
we are dealing with a threshold that is stepped on,
what difference is it to me if it is within four cubits,
what difference is it to me if it is beyond four cubits?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבה's explanation in step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's claim that the leniency is a special allowance because of בזיון on a walked-on threshold
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The danger of disgrace does not depend on distance, yet the ברייתא distinguishes between within and beyond four אמות.

steps.title: אביי sets up a new case: a threshold that is a כרמלית
steps.stepSummary: אביי sets aside רבה's approach. He explains that the משנה is talking about a threshold that is a כרמלית, with a רשות הרבים passing in front of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, אביי said: Here we are dealing with a threshold that is a כרמלית, and a רשות הרבים passes in front of it.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי replaces רבה's explanation with a new picture of the case. This step only sets up the scene; the next step explains the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלא shows that רבה's 'disgrace' reason has been dropped. Now the threshold is a כרמלית, a rabbinic in-between area. The house is on one side of it and the רשות הרבים is on the other. This setup lets the four-אמות limit make sense in terms of the carrying laws of שבת.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather. The earlier explanation is set aside and a new one is offered.
Threshold or doorstep
An in-between area. Carrying there is forbidden only מדרבנן.
Public domain. Carrying here is forbidden מן התורה.

phrases.english: Rather, Abaye said:
Here we are dealing with a threshold that is a karmelit,
phrases.notes: It is at least four טפחים wide but less than ten טפחים high.

phrases.english: and a public domain passes in front of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: הָכָא בְּאִיסְקוּפָּה כַּרְמְלִית עָסְקִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After אביי's own challenge in step 5 knocks out רבה's 'disgrace' explanation, he offers a replacement case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The threshold is walked on, and the worry is disgrace to the כתבי הקודש. Under that reading, distance should not matter.
steps.terutzMaskana: The threshold is a כרמלית in front of a רשות הרבים, so the worry is about violating the carrying laws of שבת.

steps.title: Why the four-אמות limit matters in אביי's case
steps.stepSummary: Within four אמות, carrying the ספר back would break only a rabbinic rule, so rolling it back was allowed. Beyond four אמות, carrying it back would bring a חטאת, so rolling it back was not allowed.
steps.simpleTranslation: Within four אמות: even if the ספר falls out entirely and he carries it back, he would not become liable for a חטאת, so the חכמים permitted him to roll it back. Beyond four אמות: if he carried it back, he would become liable for a חטאת, so the חכמים did not permit him.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי uses his new case to explain the ברייתא's distinction between within and beyond four אמות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the ספר is within four אמות, picking it up and carrying it back moves it only from the רשות הרבים into a כרמלית. That is a rabbinic issue, so the חכמים let him roll it back. Beyond four אמות, carrying it back means carrying four אמות in the רשות הרבים, which is a Torah violation. So the חכמים did not let him roll it, in case he ends up carrying it.

keyTerms.meaning: Four cubits. Carrying this distance in the רשות הרבים is a Torah violation.
Liability for a sin-offering, which applies only to an accidental Torah violation
The חכמים permitted it to him

steps.whatToRemember: According to אביי, the four-אמות line is the line between a rabbinic concern (within four אמות) and a Torah concern (beyond four אמות).

phrases.english: Within four cubits,
where even if it falls and he brings it back,
he does not come to liability for a sin-offering,
phrases.notes: Bringing it from the רשות הרבים into a כרמלית is only מדרבנן.

phrases.english: the Sages permitted him.
Beyond four cubits,
where if he brings it back,
he comes to liability for a sin-offering,
phrases.notes: He would be carrying four אמות in the רשות הרבים.

phrases.english: the Sages did not permit him.

steps.triggerLanguage: תּוֹךְ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת, דְּאִי נָפֵיל וּמַיְיתִי לֵיהּ לָא אָתֵי לִידֵי חִיּוּב חַטָּאת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the case set up in step 6 to answer the four-אמות difficulty raised in step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining the distinction through a difference in severity (rabbinic versus Torah)
steps.terutzMaskana: Rolling back is allowed only where the worst possible mistake is a rabbinic violation.

steps.title: Even within four אמות, he might bring the ספר into the house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי: even within four אמות, the חכמים should forbid rolling it back, in case he carries the ספר from the רשות הרבים straight into the רשות היחיד.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, let us also make a decree within four אמות, in case he brings it in from the רשות הרבים to the רשות היחיד.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks אביי's leniency for the within-four-אמות case. It points to a different Torah violation he might come to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי allowed rolling within four אמות because carrying it would only be a rabbinic problem. But the person might pick the ספר up and walk it all the way into his house, which is a רשות היחיד. Bringing an object from the רשות הרבים into a רשות היחיד is a Torah violation, so a decree seems called for here too.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. This opens a challenge built on the previous answer.
Let us make a rabbinic decree
He brings in. This refers to carrying from one domain into another.
Private domain

phrases.english: If so,
within four cubits too, let us decree
lest he bring it in
from the public domain to the private domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, תּוֹךְ אַרְבַּע אַמּוֹת נָמֵי נִגְזַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the leniency given in step 7 for the within-four-אמות case.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that within four אמות there is no risk of a Torah violation
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: There is still a risk of carrying from the רשות הרבים into a רשות היחיד, which is a Torah violation, so a decree should apply.

steps.title: The כרמלית in between does not help, based on רבא's rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks a possible defense, that the כרמלית in between breaks the transfer. It quotes רבא: carrying from the start to the end of four אמות through the air above one's head is still liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say: since a כרמלית separates the two domains, we have no problem with it. But didn't רבא say: one who carries an object from the beginning of four אמות to the end of four אמות, and carries it by way of the space above his head, is liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא predicts a possible answer for אביי and immediately knocks it down using a teaching of רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One might say that passing through the כרמלית breaks the move from the רשות הרבים to the רשות היחיד. רבא teaches otherwise: an object carried four אמות in the רשות הרבים through the exempt air above ten טפחים still makes the carrier liable. What counts is where the object starts and where it ends. In the same way, passing through a כרמלית should not prevent liability. This makes the challenge in step 8 stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you will say. This introduces a possible answer that will then be rejected.
Separates or interrupts
One who carries an object across a distance
By way of the space above him, higher than ten טפחים

steps.confusionAlert: רבא's case is not about bringing an object into a house. It is about carrying four אמות inside the רשות הרבים. The גמרא only borrows its principle: passing through an exempt middle area does not cancel liability.

phrases.english: And if you will say:
since a karmelit separates,
we have no problem with it,
but didn't Rava say:
One who carries an object
from the beginning of four cubits to the end of four,
and carried it by way of above him, is liable.
phrases.notes: He is liable even though the object passed through air above ten טפחים, which is an exempt area.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא כֵּיוָן דְּמַפְסֶקֶת כַּרְמְלִית לֵית לַן בַּהּ, וְהָאָמַר רָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the קשיא in step 8 by closing off a likely defense.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The possible defense that the כרמלית in between prevents a Torah-level transfer
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: רבא's rule shows that passing through an exempt middle area does not break liability. What matters is where the object starts and ends.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the principle that the path an object takes does not cancel liability, as long as it moves from one forbidden point to another. The answers in steps 10–15 work around this by showing why he will not carry the ספר straight through.

steps.title: The threshold is long, so he will remember
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers Step 8's worry. The משנה is talking about a long threshold, and while he walks along it he will remember not to carry the ספר inside.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A long threshold. In the meantime, while he walks along it, he will remember.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 8 by limiting the case to a long threshold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 8 worried that he would carry the ספר from the רשות הרבים straight into the רשות היחיד without thinking. If the threshold (the כרמלית) is long, crossing it takes time. During that time he will remember that he may not bring it into the private domain. So the חכמים had no reason to forbid rolling it back.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here? (a formula that narrows the case)
A long, extended threshold
In the meantime
He remembers

phrases.english: Here, with what are we dealing?
With a long threshold.
In the meantime, he will remember.
phrases.notes: While crossing the long threshold, he will recall not to bring it inside.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 8, after Step 9 blocked the simpler defense.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The threshold might be short, so he would carry the ספר straight through without thinking.
steps.terutzMaskana: The threshold is long, which gives him time to remember the prohibition.

steps.title: Even a short threshold works, because people stop to look over holy writings
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the threshold may be short, but a person normally stops to look over holy writings before putting them away. That pause on the threshold breaks any direct transfer.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: really it is a threshold that is not long. But usually a person looks over holy writings and only then puts them away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second answer that works even if the threshold is short.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not need a long threshold. It relies on normal behavior: someone holding כתבי הקודש usually stops to look at them before putting them down. That stop happens on the threshold (the כרמלית), so the ספר never goes directly from the רשות הרבים into the רשות היחיד.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you wish, say (introduces an alternative answer)
Actually, really
Sacred writings
He looks them over carefully

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
Actually, it is a threshold that is not long,
but ordinarily, sacred writings,
one looks them over and then puts them away.
phrases.notes: He pauses on the threshold to look at them.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: לְעוֹלָם בְּאִסְקוּפָּה שֶׁאֵינָהּ אֲרוּכָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to Step 8's worry, in place of Step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A short threshold gives him no chance to stop before bringing it inside.
steps.terutzMaskana: He normally stops to look over holy writings, so he pauses on the threshold.

steps.title: Maybe he stops to read in the public domain instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the second answer. Perhaps he stops to look at the scrolls while still in the רשות הרבים, and then carries them straight into the רשות היחיד.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we should worry that maybe he looks them over in the public domain, and then brings them directly into the private domain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks Step 11's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 assumed that the pause would happen on the threshold. But the pause could just as easily happen in the רשות הרבים. After that, he might walk straight through the threshold into the רשות היחיד without stopping, which brings back Step 8's worry.

keyTerms.meaning: But let us be concerned
He brings in
Directly

phrases.english: But let us be concerned that perhaps
he looks them over in the public domain
and brings them directly into the private domain.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֵיחוּשׁ דִּילְמָא מְעַיֵּין בְּהוּ בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 11's claim that the pause to look at the scrolls breaks the direct transfer
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The pause may happen in the רשות הרבים instead of on the threshold, so there could still be a direct transfer into the רשות היחיד.

steps.title: The משנה follows בן עזאי: walking counts as standing
steps.stepSummary: The משנה follows בן עזאי, who holds that someone walking is treated as if he is standing. So walking through the threshold counts as stopping there, and the ספר never goes directly into the רשות היחיד.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this? It is בן עזאי, who said: one who walks is considered like one who stands.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers Step 12 by saying that the משנה follows the opinion of בן עזאי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to בן עזאי, every step a person takes counts as if he stopped and stood in that spot. So even if he walks straight through the threshold without pausing, he is considered to have 'rested' in the כרמלית. Because of that, there is no direct transfer from the רשות הרבים to the רשות היחיד, and nothing for the חכמים to worry about.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose view is this?
A תנא
Walking is considered like standing

steps.confusionAlert: Step 9 (רבא) showed that simply passing through an in-between area does not break liability. The גמרא does not argue with that here. With 'הָא מַנִּי' it assigns the משנה to בן עזאי, who holds that walking counts as stopping, so the ספר is treated as if it actually rested in the כרמלית. The חכמים who disagree with בן עזאי would not accept this answer.

phrases.english: Whose view is this? It is בן עזאי,
who said:
One who walks is considered like one who stands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigning the משנה to a specific תנא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Walking straight through the threshold would count as a direct transfer.
steps.terutzMaskana: According to בן עזאי, walking through counts as standing in the כרמלית, so the transfer is broken.

steps.title: Maybe he will throw the scrolls in
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again. Perhaps he will throw the scrolls into the רשות היחיד, and רבי יוחנן said that בן עזאי agrees a thrower is liable.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe he will throw them in, as רבי יוחנן said: בן עזאי agrees about one who throws.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges Step 13's answer by raising the case of throwing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בן עזאי's rule only works for walking. A thrown object never 'stands' anywhere in between. רבי יוחנן says that בן עזאי himself agrees that throwing from the רשות הרבים into the רשות היחיד is liable. So the worry about a direct transfer comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: He throws
An אמורא
Agrees, concedes

phrases.english: But perhaps he will throw them,
as רבי יוחנן said:
בן עזאי agrees regarding one who throws.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer given in Step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: Step 13's reliance on בן עזאי's rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: בן עזאי's rule does not cover throwing, so throwing the scrolls would still be a direct transfer.

steps.title: People do not throw holy writings
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בר אהבה answers that this shows one does not throw holy writings. Throwing them would be disrespectful, so there is no need to worry about it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא בר אהבה said: This teaches that one does not throw sacred writings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the back-and-forth. רב אחא בר אהבה answers Step 14 and draws a halachic lesson from the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Throwing כתבי הקודש is disrespectful, so people simply do not do it. Because of that, the חכמים did not need to make a rule against a possible throw. From the fact that the משנה is not worried about throwing, רב אחא learns a rule: one may not throw holy writings.

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא
This teaches, this implies
One does not throw

steps.whatToRemember: The full chain is: long threshold → or a pause to look at the scrolls → following בן עזאי, walking counts as standing → and throwing is not a concern, because holy writings are never thrown.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a practical halacha that is still followed: one may not throw ספרי קודש, because it is disrespectful.

phrases.english: רב אחא בר אהבה said:
This teaches
that one does not throw sacred writings.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אַחָא בַּר אַהֲבָה: זֹאת אוֹמֶרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 14 and closes the line of argument.
steps.terutzResolutionType: A behavioral assumption that leads to a halachic inference
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He might throw the scrolls in, which would be a direct transfer.
steps.terutzMaskana: Holy writings are not thrown, so there is no worry about throwing.

steps.title: Is it really allowed to turn a holy scroll face-down?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about reading on a roof. The משנה tells the reader to turn the scroll over onto its writing. The גמרא challenges this from a ברייתא that forbids scribes from turning parchment face-down.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If he was reading on top of the roof, etc.' (and it said he should turn the scroll over onto its writing). But is that allowed? A ברייתא teaches that scribes writing ספרים, תפילין and מזוזות were not allowed to turn a sheet face-down. Instead, they must spread a cloth over it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new piece of the משנה, the case of reading on a roof. It immediately challenges the משנה's instruction to turn the scroll face-down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that once the scroll falls within ten טפחים of the רשות הרבים, the reader should flip it so the writing faces down. A ברייתא says that putting holy writing face-down is disrespectful, so scribes must cover it with a cloth instead. So how can our משנה tell him to do exactly what the ברייתא forbids?

keyTerms.meaning: On top of the roof (a private domain)
And is it permitted? (a challenge formula)
Scribes who write holy scrolls
A sheet of parchment
He spreads a cloth over it

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'וּמִי שְׁרֵי' attack the part of the משנה hidden in the 'וְכוּ׳': turning the scroll face-down. They do not attack reading on the roof itself.

phrases.english: 'If he was reading on top of the roof, etc.'
phrases.notes: Quote of the משנה. The 'etc.' includes the instruction to turn the scroll onto its writing.

phrases.english: And is it permitted?
But was it not taught: writers of scrolls, tefillin and mezuzos

phrases.aramaic: לֹא הִתִּירוּ לָהֶן לְהַפֵּךְ יְרִיעָה עַל פָּנֶיהָ,
phrases.english: were not permitted to turn a sheet over on its face,
rather, he spreads a cloth over it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the threshold case (steps 1–15) to the next case in the משנה, the reader on the roof.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's instruction to turn the scroll over onto its writing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא says that turning holy parchment face-down is disrespectful and forbidden. So the משנה cannot recommend it.

steps.title: Scribes have a better option; the reader on the roof does not
steps.stepSummary: The scribe can cover his parchment with a cloth, so he must. The reader on the roof cannot reach the scroll to cover it. Leaving it exposed would be even more disrespectful, so turning it over is the lesser problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: There (the scribes), it is possible to cover it. Here (the roof), it is not possible. And if he does not turn it over, there is even more disgrace to the holy writings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains that the two cases are different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Turning a scroll face-down is not ideal, so when a better way exists, like a scribe's cloth, you must use it. On the roof, the scroll is hanging down out of reach, so it cannot be covered. Leaving the writing exposed to the street would be a bigger disgrace, so flipping it is the better of two bad choices.

keyTerms.meaning: There it is possible; here it is not possible
Disgrace to holy writings
More

steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches a key principle: when every option involves some disrespect to holy writings, we choose the option with the least disrespect.

phrases.english: There it is possible,
here it is not possible,
and if he does not turn it over,
there is more disgrace to the holy writings.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases: a better option exists in one case but not in the other.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Turning holy writing face-down is always forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: It is forbidden only when covering it is possible. When it is not possible, flipping it is better than leaving it exposed.
steps.whatToRemember: Flipping a ספר face-down is only a last resort. It is allowed when it prevents a bigger disgrace.

steps.title: Why forbid rolling it back if the scroll never landed?
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says that once the scroll is within ten טפחים of the רשות הרבים, he must turn it over instead of rolling it back. The גמרא asks why. The scroll never came to rest in the רשות הרבים.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He turns it over onto the writing' (and may not roll it back)? But the scroll did not come to rest!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new challenge on the same line of the משנה. It asks why rolling the scroll back up is forbidden at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Carrying between domains is a problem only if the object actually lands in one domain and is then lifted into another. Here the scroll is just dangling in the air and never rested anywhere in the רשות הרבים. So pulling it back up should be fine, and he should not need to flip it.

keyTerms.meaning: He turns it over onto its writing
But it did not come to rest!

phrases.english: He turns it over onto the writing?
phrases.notes: Quote of the משנה's ruling, which also implies he may not roll it back.

phrases.english: But it did not come to rest!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the same משנה line. It now challenges the ban on rolling back, not the flipping.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ban on rolling the scroll back once it is within ten טפחים of the רשות הרבים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Without the scroll resting in the רשות הרבים, there is no real transfer between domains. So there is no reason to forbid pulling it back.

steps.title: רבא: the scroll is resting on a slanted wall
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that the משנה is talking about a slanted wall. The scroll lies on the slope within ten טפחים of the ground, so it does come to rest in the רשות הרבים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is talking about a slanted wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge by explaining what physical situation the משנה is describing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the wall slopes, the falling scroll lies against it instead of hanging in the air. That spot is within ten טפחים of the street, so the scroll has 'landed' in the רשות הרבים. Pulling it back up would then look like carrying from the רשות הרבים into the רשות היחיד.

keyTerms.meaning: A slanted, inclined wall
רבא, the אמורא who gives this answer

phrases.english: Rava said: With a slanted wall.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Setting the case (אוקימתא) in a specific physical situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The scroll is dangling in the air and never rested.
steps.terutzMaskana: The scroll lies on a slanted wall, so it rests within the רשות הרבים.

steps.title: אביי: then why does רבי יהודה allow rolling it back?
steps.stepSummary: אביי challenges רבא from the end of the משנה. There רבי יהודה lets him roll the scroll back even when it is a thread's width from the ground. On a slanted wall, the scroll would be resting there too.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to him: How did you explain our משנה? As a slanted wall? Then look at the end of the משנה. רבי יהודה says: even if it is lifted from the ground only a thread's width, he rolls it back to himself. But according to you, it is resting!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבא's answer. He shows that it does not fit the last part of the same משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה allows pulling the scroll back as long as it has not actually touched the ground, even if it is very close. If the case is a slanted wall, the scroll is already lying on the wall whether or not it touches the ground. So it has rested either way, and רבי יהודה's ruling would make no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: How did you set up (explain) the case?
Look at the end of the משנה
The width of a thread
He rolls it back to himself
אביי, who challenges רבא

steps.confusionAlert: אביי is not arguing with רבי יהודה. He is using רבי יהודה's ruling to show that רבא's slanted-wall explanation cannot be the setting of the משנה.

phrases.english: Abaye said to him: How did you set up our Mishnah?
With a slanted wall?
Say the end clause: Rabbi Yehudah says:
Even if it is not lifted from the ground
except by a thread's width —
he rolls it back to himself,
but it is resting!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ אַבָּיֵי: בְּמַאי אוֹקֵימְתָּא לְמַתְנִיתִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer in step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's explanation that the משנה is about a slanted wall.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: On a slanted wall the scroll rests whether or not it touches the ground. Yet רבי יהודה permits rolling it back when it is a thread's width above the ground. That shows the משנה is not about a resting scroll.

steps.title: The משנה is missing words: the first rule is about a slanted wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends רבא by saying the משנה is incomplete. The rule of turning the scroll over is only for a slanted wall. The word 'אבל' opens a contrasting case that continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה is missing words, and this is what it means to teach: When is this rule said? With a slanted wall. But...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers אביי by saying the משנה left out some words. It starts to fill them in: the 'turn it over' rule is only about a slanted wall. The final word 'אבל' sets up a contrasting case that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי's problem was that on a slanted wall the scroll would rest even at a thread's width, so רבי יהודה could not allow rolling it back. The answer splits the משנה into two cases. On a slanted wall, he turns it over. On a non-slanted wall, the scroll just hangs in the air and never rests, so a more lenient rule can apply there.

keyTerms.meaning: 'It is missing words.' The text is incomplete and must be filled in.
'And this is what it teaches.' This introduces the corrected reading.
'In what case were these words said?' This limits a rule to a specific case.
A slanted or sloping wall that the scroll can lie on.

steps.confusionAlert: 'חסורי מיחסרא' does not mean the משנה is wrong. It means the משנה is written briefly, and the גמרא spells out what it means. Also, this passage ends at 'אבל' in the middle of a sentence. The contrasting case comes in the next words.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer lets רבא's slanted-wall explanation stand. It also shows that רבי יהודה's lenient ruling belongs to a different physical setup.

phrases.english: It is missing words, and this is what it teaches:
phrases.notes: This is the standard formula for filling in a shortened משנה.

phrases.english: In what case is this said?
phrases.notes: It refers back to the rule of turning the scroll over onto its writing.

phrases.english: With a slanted wall. But…
phrases.notes: 'אבל' opens the contrasting case, which continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge in step 20 and defends רבא's explanation from step 19.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Textual emendation (חסורי מיחסרא). The משנה is split into two distinct cases: a slanted wall and a wall that is not slanted.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole משנה, including רבי יהודה's thread's-width ruling, is about one case, the slanted wall. On that reading, רבי יהודה would be allowing him to roll back a scroll that is resting in the רשות הרבים.
steps.terutzMaskana: The 'turn it over' rule is limited to a slanted wall. A contrasting case, introduced by 'אבל', covers a wall that is not slanted, where the scroll does not rest.
